title: Isandro and the Alibi
premise: Marguerite Joubert, the coroner of Saint-Aubin-le-Brûlé, receives a confession letter for a drowning ruled accidental thirty years ago—postmarked the day after the victim's memorial. The letter names no one but describes details only the killer could know, and Marguerite realizes her own late father's alibi for that night was always suspiciously perfect. As she quietly reopens the case, she finds the town's most beloved families built their lives on that old lie, and the anniversary dinner of the founding vineyard becomes the stage where thirty years of silence finally breaks. In the end, Marguerite must choose between prosecuting a dying man and letting the truth simply be spoken aloud at last.
about_author: Felix Thackeray is the pen name of a former rural registrar who spent two decades filing other people's endings before writing his own. He lives above a shuttered notary's office and claims he can date any photograph by the shape of its shadows.

chapters.title: Postmarked Grief
chapters.summary: Marguerite, sorting the last effects of drowned boy Émile Roche thirty years after his death, opens an unsigned confession letter that arrived one day after his memorial. Her POV; the beat is quiet dread—the letter knows things never written in any file, including the color of Émile's shoelaces.

chapters.title: The Grave Registry
chapters.summary: Marguerite walks the cemetery she knows by heart, rereading Émile's headstone and her father's old coroner notes. Flashbacks reveal her father signed the accidental-drowning ruling after a single night's inquiry. Her POV; the beat is dawning suspicion turned inward, toward family.

chapters.title: Alibis of the Vintage
chapters.summary: Marguerite interviews the four witnesses from 1994, all now pillars of the Delacour vineyard dynasty: the patriarch Henri, his son Baptiste, the housekeeper Sylvie, and the priest Père Anselme. Their stories align too neatly. Rotating POVs; the beat is polished surfaces hiding hairline cracks.

chapters.title: What the River Keeps
chapters.summary: Marguerite dredges her memory of being fourteen that summer—she saw Émile alive near the mill race hours after the 'official' time of death. Her POV interleaved with Émile's final day in third person; the beat is vertigo, the timeline itself beginning to lie.

chapters.title: A Second Letter
chapters.summary: Another envelope arrives: this one addressed to Henri Delacour, returned undelivered to Marguerite by the postmistress. Inside, a threat, not a confession. Marguerite's POV with a tense scene of Henri burning papers; the beat is escalation—the confessor wants something more than absolution.

chapters.title: Sylvie's Silence
chapters.summary: The aging housekeeper finally speaks: she saw Baptiste and Émile fighting over money the night Émile died, and was paid to forget. Sylvie's POV; the beat is guilt surfacing like a body after decades underwater, tender and terrified.

chapters.title: The Father's Alibi
chapters.summary: Marguerite uncovers her father's diary: he falsified the time of death to protect someone he loved—Henri's late wife, Camille, who was with him that night. Her POV; the beat is betrayal and grief colliding, the investigator becoming the investigated.

chapters.title: Anniversary Eve
chapters.summary: On the eve of the vineyard's thirtieth-anniversary dinner, Marguerite confronts Baptiste, who confesses to the fight but swears Émile was alive when he left—and produces a witness no one expected: Père Anselme, who gave Émile shelter and watched him walk toward the river at dawn. Dual POV; the beat is the truth reshuffling like cards.

chapters.title: The Toast
chapters.summary: At the anniversary dinner, the confessor stands: it is Camille's sister Odile, who has waited thirty years to force the truth into daylight. She reads the letters aloud before the whole town. Climax; rotating POVs converge; the beat is public reckoning—Émile died saving himself from the river's floodgate, but every adult present let the lie stand because it suited them.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Marguerite files a corrected finding—not murder, but negligence and concealment—and chooses not to prosecute the dying and the elderly, letting records and memory carry the sentence instead. She carves Émile's true story into the registry. Her POV; the beat is bittersweet belonging: justice outside the law, and a town that must live with what it now knows.
